language_wrapper: A long hallway contains {n} closed lockers labeled 1 through {n}. A student begins at locker 1, facing right. He repeatedly walks back and forth between the ends of the hallway. On each pass, starting from the end he currently occupies, he opens the first closed locker he encounters and then continues using the fixed pattern: opens {r} consecutive closed lockers, then skips {s} consecutive closed lockers, counting only closed lockers and ignoring already-open ones. When he reaches an end, he immediately turns around and begins the next pass, again starting by opening the first closed locker he encounters and then repeating the same pattern. He continues until every locker is open. What is the number of the last locker he opens?
hardness_rationale: The seed problem corresponds to alternating elimination with step 2 on a line, starting by opening one and then skipping one. This family generalizes the action to periodic blocks: open r consecutive closed lockers and skip s consecutive closed lockers, counting only closed lockers and resetting the pattern at each turn. The back-and-forth traversal combined with block deletions creates a nontrivial alternating-direction sieve on an ordered set: parity, endpoints, and block-length interactions jointly determine the survivors across passes. Solving requires modeling the process as alternating-direction block elimination and tracking the evolution of the ordered list of closed lockers, which is substantially more intricate than the seed’s simple every-other rule. Closed-form solutions are generally out of reach; instead, one must employ invariant reasoning or derive recurrences to follow the survivors—significantly harder than the seed’s binary/parity argument.
notes: Proof of correctness for the verifier’s computation: Let L_0 = [1,2, ..., n] denote the ordered list of closed lockers before any action. Define the elimination operator E_{\rightarrow}^{r,s}(L) on an ordered list L traversed left-to-right as: delete (open) r consecutive elements, then keep (skip) s consecutive elements, and repeat until the end; counting is performed only on the sequence of still-closed elements. Similarly, the right-to-left operator E_{\leftarrow}^{r,s}(L) is defined by first reversing L, applying E_{\rightarrow}^{r,s}, then reversing back. Each pass of the student exactly implements E_{\rightarrow}^{r,s} or E_{\leftarrow}^{r,s} on the current set of closed lockers because: (i) the student starts each pass by opening the first closed locker encountered, hence the pattern begins with an opening block; (ii) only closed lockers contribute to the open/skip counts, as already-open lockers are ignored; (iii) upon reaching an end, the student reverses direction, and the next pass applies the same block rule in the opposite order. Therefore, after k passes the set of closed lockers equals L_k = E_{d_k}^{r,s}(L_{k-1}), where d_k alternates between rightward and leftward directions. Because r \ge 1, at least one closed locker is opened on any pass that encounters a closed locker, so the process strictly decreases the number of closed lockers; thus it terminates with exactly one closed locker remaining after some finite number of passes. That unique survivor, say x, is the last closed locker to be opened, and it is opened during the final pass; hence x is the last locker opened. The verifier simulates this process exactly: it iterates over the hallway in the current direction, updating open/skip counters only when encountering closed lockers, toggling between opening r and skipping s closed lockers, and resetting the pattern at each turnaround. It maintains the invariant that no locker is opened more than once and that open/skip counts apply solely to closed lockers. Consequently, the returned locker index equals the unique survivor of the alternating-direction block elimination, i.e., the last locker opened. Difficulty is additionally enforced by requiring at least three passes and excluding edge outcomes to avoid trivial instances.
source_question: A bored student walks down a hall that contains a row of closed lockers, numbered 1 to 1024. He opens the locker numbered 1, and then alternates between skipping and opening each locker thereafter. When he reaches the end of the hall, the student turns around and starts back. He opens the first closed locker he encounters, and then alternates between skipping and opening each closed locker thereafter. The student continues wandering back and forth in this manner until every locker is open. What is the number of the last locker he opens?
